answer: The statutory rule is that “the registration of title to every land parcel under this Act shall be in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” So, for a parcel being brought under the title-registration system, the registration of title must follow the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.

When the Commissioner of Title Settlement receives the certified copies of cadastral maps, he or she must “publish a Notice in the Gazette,” and that Notice must call for any claimants to the land parcel specified in the Notice to submit their claims within a prescribed period from the date of publication of the Notice. After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must cause an investigation to be conducted to determine the genuineness or otherwise of those claims.

The Act provides two different procedures.

1. **Reference of disputed claims for determination**: If, during the course of investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, due to the disputed nature of the claims, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination to the District Court** having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. This is a reference made by the Commissioner, based on the disputed nature of the claims. [node_id: 21-1998/section-21]

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant**: Any claimant aggrieved by any Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 may **prefer an appeal against such declaration within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. This is a claimant-initiated appeal against a declaration, and it must be made within the prescribed period. [node_id: 21-1998/section-22]

So, the first procedure is a **Commissioner-led reference for investigation and determination** because of disputed claims; the second is a **claimant-led appeal** against a declaration, made within the prescribed period.

The statutory rule is that an interest in a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act is not acquired unless the title or interest is registered under that Act. Also, a land parcel, title to which has been registered under the Act, or any interest in it, can be transferred or dealt with only in accordance with the Act, and “every disposition otherwise effected shall be void.” An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act “shall take effect on registration” of the instrument under the Act.

Applied here, Nimal executed an instrument purporting to transfer an interest in a land parcel registered under the Act, but the instrument was not registered. On those facts, the transferee did not acquire the interest, because the interest is not entitled to be held unless registered, and the disposition otherwise effected is void. The instrument would take legal effect only upon registration under the Act.

Under s 48, “Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.”

Applied here, the registered owner executed one instrument purporting to convey the parcel to two purchasers as owners in common. On those facts, the instrument is void and it shall not be registered under the Act, unless it is made in accordance with some other provision of the Act, which is not stated in the facts.

The statutory rule is that, for land or interests in land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance “shall not apply,” and the Partition Act also “shall not apply.”

Applied here, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, a claim to ownership by prescription cannot be made under the Prescription Ordinance in relation to that parcel, and a partition action under the Partition Act cannot be instituted in respect of that parcel.

Under section 59, a Court may order rectification where it is satisfied that a registration has been obtained by fraud, but the proviso says the Court shall not order rectification so as to affect the title of a registered owner who is in possession and who has acquired the land parcel for valuable consideration, unless that owner was a party to the fraud. On the facts given, the present registered owner is in possession, acquired the parcel for valuable consideration, and was not a party to the fraud, so the Court may not rectify the register against that owner.

As to indemnity, section 60(1) says a person suffering loss or damage or who has been prejudiced by reason of not rectifying the Register in consequence of an order of Court made under section 59 shall, on an order of Court, be entitled to be indemnified by the Government out of the Insurance Fund. Section 60(2) prevents indemnity if the person has himself caused or substantially contributed to the fraud, or derives title from such a person. On the stated facts, the person who suffered loss may claim indemnity if the loss was caused by non-rectification in consequence of a section 59 court order, and there is no stated fact showing the section 60(2) bar applies.

The Act requires these steps:

1. When the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General. He must then file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title, and forward the duplicate of the condominium plan together with the owner’s application to the appropriate Registrar of Title.

2. If the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the application conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File; open a new title register for each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross-references in the register in which the land parcel is registered; record in the Property Section that the land comprised therein consists only of common property; record in the Encumbrances Section that registers in respect of condominium parcels have been opened; inform the applicant that the condominium parcels have been registered and notify him of the reference numbers of the relevant registers; and issue a Certificate of Title after recovery of the prescribed fees.

On the background given, the plan has been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, so these are the principal statutory steps for filing the plan and registering the condominium parcels.

Under section 22, when a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, “the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property.” Under section 23, the remaining inheritance goes next to “descendants.” Section 24 says that “Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents,” that “all the children take equally per capita,” and that “the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.”

Applied here:
- The surviving spouse takes 1/2 of the estate.
- The other 1/2 is for the descendants.
- There is one living child and one deceased child’s branch represented by two grandchildren.
- The living child takes one stirpital share of the descendants’ half.
- The two grandchildren together take the other stirpital share, by representation, and divide it equally.

Calculation:
- Estate remaining after spouse’s half = 1/2
- Divide that remaining 1/2 into 2 equal stirpes: 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/4 each stirpe
- Living child = 1/4 of the whole estate
- Deceased child’s branch = 1/4 of the whole estate
- Each grandchild = 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8 of the whole estate

So the shares are:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

The rule in Wills Ordinance, s 5 is that a will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka that contains a devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka is “valid and effectual to alienate and pass the property” if it was “duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed,” and was made by a person who by the law of that country or of Sri Lanka was competent to make a will.

Applied here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country where it was executed, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. Those facts satisfy s 5. Therefore, the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

The rule is that no precept or order for the service of notice or summons may be issued in proceedings or an action for enforcing a right of pre-emption until proof is furnished to the court that the proceedings or action have been registered as a lis pendens in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. In addition, at any time after the action is instituted, the court may in its discretion order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5. If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period allowed by the court, or any further periods allowed by the court not exceeding three months in the aggregate, the action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases. Applied here, the plaintiff must first furnish proof of registration of the action as a lis pendens before notice or summons can issue; the court may order deposit of the purchase amount stated in the section 5 notice; and if that deposit is not made within the allowed time, the action will be struck off the roll of pending cases.

The rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.”

Applied to the facts: the mortgage is of a physically divided portion of a tea estate as a separate lot, and it was made after the appointed day. That matches the statutory condition, so the mortgage is null and void.

No. The statute says: “No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” So the share in the common elements cannot be disposed of separately from the condominium parcel. The statute also says that “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel notwithstanding the fact that no specific or particular reference has been made thereto in the instrument or deed relating to such alienation.” So when the condominium parcel is transferred, the associated undivided share in the common elements transfers with it.

missing_evidence: The complete text of Survey Act, section 13, including the full wording of paragraph (b) and any corresponding preparation requirement for plans or maps under that paragraph, is needed to state all conditions for admissibility in evidence.

answer: Yes. The provision states that any cadastral map, plan, or other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, if it purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or any officer acting on his behalf, is “admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It also “may be taken as prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original” until evidence to the contrary is first given. Applied here, the copy purporting to be authenticated and signed by the Surveyor-General is admissible in place of the original, and its initial evidential status is prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated in it.

No. Under Companies Act, s 73, it is "not lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares" unless "a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company." Because no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered, the company may not register the voluntary transfer.

The exception is in the proviso: nothing in s 73 affects the company's power to register as shareholder or debenture holder any person to whom the right to the shares or debentures "has been transmitted by operation of law." So, where entitlement passes by operation of law, the section does not prevent registration of that person.

Under Companies Act, s 79, a certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company, and specifying shares held by a shareholder, "shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares." Applied here, a share certificate in that form has prima facie evidential effect that the recorded shareholder has title to the specified shares.

The statutory duties breached are:

1. A director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes ... the provisions contained in the articles of the company.”
2. A director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.”
3. A director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.”

Applied here, the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so the director breached the duty to comply with the company’s articles. The director also carried out the decision recklessly, so the director breached the duty not to act recklessly or grossly negligently. Finally, by failing to exercise the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that director’s knowledge and experience, the director breached the standard-of-care duty.

The Act says that “Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.” The term “alienation” includes “transfer” of land. On the facts, the transfer of land was completed in direct contravention of the Act, so that alienation is void and has no legal effect.
